u1s1: The memory cell is the fundamental building block of computer memory.
u2s1: The memory cell is a device, such as an electronic circuit, that stores one bit of binary information and it must be set to store a logic 1 (high voltage level) and reset to store a logic 0 (low voltage level).
u3s1: The value in the memory cell can be accessed by reading it.
u4s1: Over the history of computing, different memory cell architectures have been used, including core memory, twistor memory, and bubble memory.
u5s1: Today, the most common memory cell architecture is MOS memory, which consists of metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS) memory cells.
u6s1: The SRAM (static RAM) memory cell is a type of flip-flop circuit, typically implemented using MOSFETs.
u7s1: Charging and discharging a capacitor can store either a '1' or a '0' in the cell.
u8s1: Most non-volatile memory (NVM), on the other hand, is based on floating-gate memory cell architectures.
u9s1: Non-volatile memory technologies such as EPROM, EEPROM, and flash memory utilize floating-gate memory cells, which rely on floating-gate MOSFET transistors.
u10s1: == Description == The memory cell is the fundamental building block of memory.
u11s1: Regardless of the implementation technology used, the purpose of the binary memory cell is always the same.
u12s1: It stores one bit of binary information that can be accessed by reading the cell and it must be set to store a 1 and reset to store a 0.
u13s1: == Significance == Logic circuits without memory cells are called combinational, meaning the output depends only on the present input.
u14s1: In computers, it allows to store both programs and data and memory cells are also used for temporary storage of the output of combinational circuits to be used later by digital systems.
u15s1: Logic circuits that use memory cells are called sequential circuits, meaning the output depends not only on the present input, but also on the history of past inputs.
u16s1: This dependence on the history of past inputs makes these circuits stateful and it is the memory cells that store this state.
u17s1: Computer memory used in most contemporary computer systems is built mainly out of DRAM cells; since the layout is much smaller than SRAM, it can be more densely packed yielding cheaper memory with greater capacity.
u18s1: Since the DRAM memory cell stores its value as the charge of a capacitor, and there are current leakage issues, its value must be constantly rewritten.
u19s1: This is one of the reasons that make DRAM cells slower than the larger SRAM (static RAM) cells, which has its value always available.
u20s1: Semiconductor memory began in the early 1960s with bipolar memory cells, made of bipolar transistors.
u21s1: === MOS memory cells === In 1957, Frosch and Derick were able to manufacture the first silicon dioxide field effect transistors at Bell Labs, the first transistors in which drain and source were adjacent at the surface.
u22s1: The invention of the MOSFET enabled the practical use of metal–oxide–semiconductor (MOS) transistors as memory cell storage elements, a function previously served by magnetic cores.
u23s1: The first modern memory cells were introduced in 1964, when John Schmidt designed the first 64-bit p-channel MOS (PMOS) static random-access memory (SRAM).
u24s1: SRAM typically has six-transistor cells, whereas DRAM (dynamic random-access memory) typically has single-transistor cells.
u25s1: In 1965, Toshiba's Toscal BC-1411 electronic calculator used a form of capacitive bipolar DRAM, storing 180-bit data on discrete memory cells, consisting of germanium bipolar transistors and capacitors.
u26s1: This led to his development of a single-transistor DRAM memory cell.
u27s1: In 1967, Dennard filed a patent for a single-transistor DRAM memory cell, based on MOS technology.
u28s1: DRAM chips during the early 1970s had three-transistor cells, before single-transistor cells became standard since the mid-1970s.
u29s1: The two most common types of DRAM memory cells since the 1980s have been trench-capacitor cells and stacked-capacitor cells.
u30s1: Trench-capacitor cells are where holes (trenches) are made in a silicon substrate, whose side walls are used as a memory cell, whereas stacked-capacitor cells are the earliest form of three-dimensional memory (3D memory), where memory cells are stacked vertically in a three-dimensional cell structure.
u31s1: === Floating-gate MOS memory cells === The floating-gate MOSFET (FGMOS) was invented by Dawon Kahng and Simon Sze at Bell Labs in 1967.
u32s1: They proposed the concept of floating-gate memory cells, using FGMOS transistors, which could be used to produce reprogrammable ROM (read-only memory).
u33s1: Floating-gate memory cells later became the basis for non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies including EPROM (erasable programmable ROM), EEPROM (electrically erasable programmable ROM) and flash memory.
u34s1: Multi-level cell (MLC) flash memory was introduced by NEC, which demonstrated quad-level cells in a 64 Mb flash chip storing 2-bit per cell in 1996.
u35s1: 3D V-NAND, where flash memory cells are stacked vertically using 3D charge trap flash (CTP) technology, was first announced by Toshiba in 2007, and first commercially manufactured by Samsung Electronics in 2013.

u42s1: === Floating gate === Floating-gate memory cells, based on floating-gate MOSFETs, are used for most non-volatile memory (NVM) technologies, including EPROM, EEPROM and flash memory.
u43s1: According to R. Bez and A. Pirovano: A floating-gate memory cell is basically an MOS transistor with a gate completely surrounded by dielectrics (Fig. 1.2), the floating-gate (FG), and electrically governed by a capacitive-coupled control-gate (CG).
u44s1: Being electrically isolated, the FG acts as the storing electrode for the cell device.
u45s1: Charge injected into the FG is maintained there, allowing modulation of the ‘apparent’ threshold voltage (i.e. VT seen from the CG) of the cell transistor.
